title: Three Women and a Small Boy beneath a Wisteria Arbor
recordTitle: Three Women and a Small Boy beneath a Wisteria Arbor on the Bank of a Stream
medium: One sheet of a triptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Francis Lathrop Collection, Purchase, Frederick C. Hewitt Fund, 1911
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A Japanese woodblock print of three women in long patterned robes and a small boy, gathered together near a stream beneath a framework covered with wisteria.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, culture, public-domain flag, credit line, tags (Boys, Women, Rivers) and image URLs read from the record

context: A color woodblock print by Torii Kiyonaga, dated to about 1790. The record describes it as one sheet of a triptych, so it was designed to be seen side by side with two other sheets.

descriptions.k: Three women and a little boy sit near a stream. Flowers hang over them like a leafy roof. The women wear long robes with patterns. What do you think they are talking about?
descriptions.g12: A long time ago in Japan, an artist named Kiyonaga made this print. Three women and a small boy relax by a stream under hanging flowers called wisteria. Look at their long robes and the patterns on them. This print was one part of a set of three. What might be happening in the other two parts?
descriptions.g35: Torii Kiyonaga made this woodblock print around 1790 in Japan. It shows three women and a small boy outdoors beside a stream, under a framework hung with wisteria blossoms. Notice their long, flowing robes and the way the figures are grouped. This is one sheet of three that were meant to hang side by side. Why might an artist split a scene into three parts?
descriptions.g68: Kiyonaga was one of the leading designers of Japanese woodblock prints around 1790, known for tall, graceful figures in everyday outings. Here, three women and a boy gather by a stream under wisteria. The robes, with their patterns and flowing lines, are as important as the setting. Because this is only one sheet of a triptych, the scene continues beyond its edges. How does that design shape the way you look at it?
descriptions.g910: This sheet from a triptych presents leisure by a stream as an elegant, carefully staged moment. Kiyonaga's figures are tall and balanced, and the patterned robes create rhythm across the surface, while the wisteria and water frame the group. Because the composition was designed to continue across other sheets, the edges are part of the idea. How do line, pattern and the triptych format work together to turn an outing into a design?
descriptions.g1112: Kiyonaga's triptych sheet belongs to the Edo-period market for woodblock prints of fashionable daily life. The tall, composed figures and patterned robes can be read as a celebration of elegance, a record of contemporary fashion, or an idealized version of leisure. The format asks us to imagine a continuing scene across sheets. How does that incompleteness affect what the single sheet can claim to show, and what should a viewer be cautious about assuming?

teacherNote.context: Torii Kiyonaga designed prints of fashionable daily life in Edo-period Japan. This sheet is one part of a triptych, three prints meant to be viewed together.
directions: Have students imagine and sketch the missing sheets to the left and right.
Ask students to trace two lines of a robe and describe how line alone suggests cloth.
Compare the way this print and another artwork in the archive suggest outdoor space.
